CHIEF COMPLAINT
Positive hepatitis C antibody screening test

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient presented for evaluation following positive hepatitis C (HCV) antibody test discovered during routine physical examination screening. Patient reports being surprised by the diagnosis as he has been feeling well and asymptomatic. He denies any prior knowledge of hepatitis C infection. He has a significant remote history of intravenous drug use but reports being clean for over 15 years. He continues to consume alcohol, approximately one beer daily, which is less than his previous use. Patient continues to smoke approximately 1-2 cigarettes per day and reports difficulty quitting. He is married with children.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient denies current symptoms and reports feeling well overall.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No other significant medical conditions reported.

MEDICATIONS
Patient reports taking no current medications.

ALLERGIES
Not documented

FAMILY HISTORY
Significant for hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and depression

SOCIAL HISTORY
Former intravenous drug user, clean for greater than 15 years. Current tobacco use approximately 1-2 cigarettes per day. Alcohol use approximately one beer daily. Married with children.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs reviewed and within normal limits. General: Patient in no distress, no jaundice noted. Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm with grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur appreciated. Pulmonary: Lungs clear without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi. Abdomen: Bowel sounds present, soft, no hepatosplenomegaly. Neurological: No gait disturbance or edema noted.

RESULTS
HCV antibody positive. Liver function panel with elevated AST at 39 units; ALT, albumin, and total bilirubin all within normal limits.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Hepatitis C infection. Patient counseled that hepatitis C is a viral infection affecting the liver and likely has been present for several years, as most patients remain asymptomatic until advanced disease. Plan includes: (1) Confirm diagnosis with HCV RNA testing and HCV genotype determination; (2) Assess severity of liver disease with hepatic ultrasound elastography to evaluate for fibrosis; (3) Screen family members (wife and children) with HCV antibody test and coordinate appointments with their primary care physician; (4) Follow-up appointment in three weeks to review test results and determine treatment plan; (5) Counseled on importance of smoking cessation as both hepatitis C and smoking are harmful to liver health.
